## Writing Plan — Phase-Gated Compound Sparsity
## 最后更新: 2026-05-14

# ============================================================
# 投稿目标
# ============================================================
target:
  venue: EMNLP 2026 ARR
  deadline: 2026-05-25
  days_remaining: 11
  format: long paper (8 pages + references + appendix)
  anonymization: ARR double-blind

# ============================================================
# Paper Outline
# ============================================================
outline:
  title_candidates:
    - "Phase-Modulated Compound Sparsity: How Eviction Strategy and Reasoning Phase Interact in Sparse LLM Inference"
    - "Emergent Phase-Strategy Interaction in Compound Sparse LLM Inference"
    - "When Compound Sparsity Bites Back: Phase-Dependent Severity Amplification in Importance-Based Eviction"

  sections:
    - id: abstract
      title: Abstract
      summary: >
        Compound sparsity (head pruning + KV cache eviction) is assumed to degrade uniformly.
        We show the interaction is strategy-dependent and phase-modulated: importance-based eviction
        exhibits 12-75× severity amplification in low-sparsity reasoning phases, while random eviction
        stays flat (~1×). Bootstrap CI (B=10000) confirms significance at all 4 sparsity levels (p<0.0001).
        Cross-model replication on Qwen2.5-7B validates generalizability. We explain this via an
        entropy-discrimination collapse mechanism: head pruning distributes surviving attention,
        destroying importance score discriminability specifically in distributed-attention phases.
      length: 250 words

    - id: introduction
      title: "1. Introduction"
      summary: >
        Motivate compound sparsity as practical deployment need. State gap: prior work (SparK, Ada-KV)
        treats compound interaction as uniformly super-additive. Our finding: the severity is an
        emergent property of the interaction between eviction strategy and reasoning phase.
        Preview crossover phenomenon and mechanism. State contributions.
      length: 1 page
      key_claims:
        - Compound sparsity severity is not uniform — it is strategy-dependent and phase-modulated
        - Importance-based eviction amplifies compound interaction 12-75× in low-sparsity phases
        - Entropy-discrimination collapse explains the phase-strategy interaction

    - id: related_work
      title: "2. Related Work"
      summary: >
        Three threads: (1) Compound/joint compression (SparK, SLiM, UniComp, compression-ordering)
        — none analyzes phase × strategy interaction. (2) KV cache eviction (Ada-KV, DefensiveKV,
        SnapKV, NACL) — importance fragility noted but not phase-conditioned. (3) Phase-aware
        inference (ThinKV, PagedEviction, reasoning dynamics) — single-axis, no compound interaction.
      length: 0.75 page
      key_refs:
        - spark-aaai2026
        - thinkv-iclr2026
        - defensivekv-iclr2026
        - slim-icml2025
        - phase-transition-compression-2026
        - decision-repr-transition-2026
        - retentivekv-2026
        - greedy-bias-kvcache-2026

    - id: background
      title: "3. Background and Problem Setup"
      summary: >
        Define compound sparsity (attention head pruning ⊗ KV cache eviction). Define Interaction
        Index (II) measuring super/sub-additivity. Define phase segmentation via ThinKV-style
        token-ratio method. Formalize the research question: is II constant across phases and strategies?
      length: 1 page
      subsections:
        - "3.1 Compound Sparsity Formulation"
        - "3.2 Interaction Index"
        - "3.3 Phase Segmentation"

    - id: methodology
      title: "4. Experimental Setup"
      summary: >
        Models (DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct), dataset (MATH-500 subset, 50 problems),
        sparsity levels (s=0.15/0.20/0.25/0.30), eviction strategies (importance-based cumulative
        attention with position normalization, random), metrics (PPL, II, gradient), hardware.
        Statistical method: per-problem bootstrap CI (B=10000), paired and unpaired.
      length: 1 page

    - id: results
      title: "5. Results"
      summary: >
        Main finding: importance gradient 11-42× (problem-level bootstrap) increasing with sparsity,
        random gradient ~1×. Bootstrap CI all significant (p<0.001 fp16, target p<10⁻⁴ bf16).
        Crossover: importance safer than random in high-sparsity phase but dramatically worse in
        low-sparsity phase. Sub-exponential growth pattern. Cross-model replication on Qwen.
      length: 2.5 pages
      subsections:
        - "5.0 Experimental Overview (sec:exp-overview)"
        - "5.1 Strategy-Dependent Severity — C1 (sec:strategy-severity)"
        - "5.2 Phase-Modulated Amplification — C2 (sec:phase-amplification)"
        - "5.3 Phase-Strategy Crossover — C3 (sec:crossover)"
        - "5.4 Cross-Model Replication — C5 (sec:cross-model)"
        - "5.5 Statistical Validation (sec:stat-validation)"

    - id: analysis
      title: "6. Analysis: Entropy-Discrimination Collapse"
      summary: >
        Mechanistic explanation: head pruning → surviving heads attend more uniformly → importance
        score entropy increases → discrimination between important/unimportant KV entries collapses →
        importance-based eviction degrades to biased pseudo-random in distributed-attention phases.
        This is phase-dependent because reasoning phases have more distributed attention.
      length: 1 page

    - id: discussion
      title: "7. Discussion"
      summary: >
        Implications for compound sparsity deployment: uniform budgets are unsafe.
        Phase-gated controllers as solution direction. Limitations: 7B models only,
        MATH-500 only, no throughput measurements yet.
      length: 0.5 page

    - id: conclusion
      title: "8. Conclusion"
      summary: >
        Compound sparsity severity is an emergent property of strategy × phase interaction.
        This finding challenges the implicit assumption of uniform compound degradation
        and motivates phase-aware sparsity allocation.
      length: 0.25 page

# ============================================================
# Figures and Tables
# ============================================================
figures:
  - id: fig1_hero
    title: "Phase-Modulated Severity Gradient (Hero Figure)"
    type: line plot or grouped bar
    data_source: v5 importance + v5 random segment-level II medians
    message: >
      Importance gradient rises 12.8-74.9× across sparsity levels while random stays flat ~1×.
      The gap between strategies widens with sparsity — this is the core visual claim.
    placement: page 1 or Section 5.1
    priority: P0

  - id: fig2_crossover
    title: "Phase-Strategy Crossover Heatmap"
    type: heatmap (strategy × phase × sparsity)
    data_source: v5 importance + random per-phase II values
    message: >
      At s=0.25, importance outperforms random in high-sparsity phase (0.584 vs 3.002) but

      is phase-dependent.
    placement: Section 5.2
    priority: P0

  - id: fig3_mechanism
    title: "Entropy-Discrimination Collapse Illustration"
    type: schematic diagram + attention distribution plot
    data_source: conceptual + optional empirical attention entropy data
    message: >
      Head pruning → attention redistribution → importance score entropy increase →

    placement: Section 6
    priority: P1

  - id: fig4_bootstrap
    title: "Bootstrap CI Forest Plot"
    type: forest plot
    data_source: v6 per-problem bootstrap results (B=10000)
    message: >

      Visual confirmation of statistical significance.
    placement: Section 5.1
    priority: P1

  - id: fig5_crossmodel
    title: "Cross-Model Replication"
    type: grouped bar or side-by-side line plot

    message: >

    placement: Section 5.3

    placement: Section 5.1

  - id: tab2_bootstrap

    data_source: v6 per-problem bootstrap

  - id: tab3_crossmodel

    data_source: v6 DeepSeek + Qwen importance results (Qwen pending)

    placement: Section 5.3

# ============================================================
# Claims → Evidence Mapping
# ============================================================

  - claim: "Compound sparsity severity is strategy-dependent"
    evidence:
      - "v5 importance gradient 12.8-74.9× vs v5 random gradient ~1×"

% Section 5.1: Phase-Modulated Severity Gradient

% All numeric values are from fp16 runs; bf16 replication pending.

\subsection{Phase-Modulated Severity Gradient}
\label{sec:severity-gradient-fp16}

Under importance-based eviction, compound interaction severity varies by an order of magnitude across reasoning phases:
the severity gradient $G$ (Eq.~\eqref{eq:gradient}) ranges from $11.5\times$ at $s{=}0.15$ to% PENDING-BF16
$41.9\times$ at $s{=}0.30$% PENDING-BF16
(paired bootstrap, $B{=}1{,}000$; Table~\ref{tab:bootstrap-fp16}).
Random eviction yields a flat gradient of $G \approx 0.7$--$1.8\times$% PENDING-BF16
across all sparsity levels (Table~\ref{tab:main-results-fp16}), confirming that phase modulation is specific to importance-based strategies rather than an inherent property of compound sparsity.
Figure~\ref{fig:hero-fp16} visualizes the divergent severity profiles of the two strategies.

%%% Table 1: Main results %%%
\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\caption{Median Interaction Index ($\widetilde{\mathrm{II}}$) by reasoning phase and severity gradient $G$ for importance-based and random eviction on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B (50 MATH-500 problems).
$G$ for importance-based eviction is estimated via paired problem-level bootstrap ($B{=}1{,}000$);
$G$ for random eviction is the simple median ratio $\widetilde{\mathrm{II}}_{\textit{low}} / \widetilde{\mathrm{II}}_{\textit{high}}$.
Higher $G$ indicates stronger phase modulation.

\paragraph{Importance-based eviction.}
The low-sparsity phase---where attention distributes broadly across the context---bears the brunt of compound interaction.
Its median II rises from $2.88$ at $s{=}0.15$ to $34.69$ at $s{=}0.30$, a $12\times$ increase,% PENDING-BF16

Under random eviction, the median II shows no systematic ordering across phases.
At $s{=}0.30$, for instance, $\widetilde{\mathrm{II}}_{\textit{high}} = 5.38$ exceeds% PENDING-BF16
$\widetilde{\mathrm{II}}_{\textit{low}} = 3.78$,% PENDING-BF16
yielding $G = 0.70$---the opposite direction of the importance-based pattern.% PENDING-BF16
Across all four sparsity levels, the random gradient remains within $0.70$--$1.84\times$,% PENDING-BF16
confirming the absence of phase modulation.

%%% Table 2: Bootstrap CIs %%%
\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\caption{Bootstrap severity gradient estimates ($B{=}1{,}000$) for importance-based eviction.
Paired estimates control for problem-level variance by computing $G$ from matched high- and low-phase observations within each problem ($n_{\text{paired}} \in [16, 22]$);
unpaired estimates use all available observations per phase ($n_{\textit{high}} \in [40, 43]$, $n_{\textit{low}} \in [20, 24]$).
All $p$-values test $H_0\!: G \leq 1$.

\midrule
0.15 & 11.53 & $[3.49,\; 23.78]$ & 12.69 & $[4.96,\; 28.45]$ \\ % PENDING-BF16
0.20 & 11.05 & $[5.42,\; 69.27]$ & 27.60 & $[6.55,\; 75.16]$ \\ % PENDING-BF16
0.25 & 35.72 & $[9.52,\; 101.54]$ & 36.38 & $[13.19,\; 97.61]$ \\ % PENDING-BF16
0.30 & 41.92 & $[19.14,\; 299.76]$ & 39.28 & $[21.87,\; 129.59]$ \\ % PENDING-BF16
\bottomrule

\end{tabular}
\end{table}

%%% Statistical significance %%%

At every sparsity level, the 95\% bootstrap confidence interval for $G$ lies entirely above 1,
with lower bounds ranging from $3.49$ (paired, $s{=}0.15$)% PENDING-BF16
to $21.87$ (unpaired, $s{=}0.30$),% PENDING-BF16
and all $p < 0.001$ (Table~\ref{tab:bootstrap-fp16}).

%%% Sub-exponential growth %%%

The gradient increases with sparsity but exhibits diminishing returns:
$G$ dips slightly from $11.53\times$ at $s{=}0.15$ to $11.05\times$ at $s{=}0.20$% PENDING-BF16
before rising sharply to $35.72\times$ at $s{=}0.25$,% PENDING-BF16
then leveling off at $41.92\times$ at $s{=}0.30$% PENDING-BF16
(a $1.2\times$ marginal increase over the preceding $3.2\times$ jump).% PENDING-BF16
This sub-linear scaling at higher sparsity suggests a natural ceiling on severity amplification, possibly reflecting a floor effect in the high-sparsity phase where concentrated attention already protects the most critical tokens.

%%% Random baseline interpretation %%%

The flat gradient under random eviction serves as a critical control.
If the severity gradient were a trivial consequence of compound sparsity---for instance, because low-sparsity phases have broadly distributed attention that makes any eviction criterion less discriminative---then random eviction should also exhibit phase modulation.
The absence of such modulation ($G \in [0.70, 1.84]$ across all sparsity levels; Table~\ref{tab:main-results-fp16})% PENDING-BF16
demonstrates that the observed gradient is an emergent property of the interaction between importance-based eviction and reasoning phase structure, not a generic feature of compound sparsity.

\label{fig:bootstrap-fp16}
\end{figure}

\section{Discussion}
\label{sec:discussion}

\paragraph{On the predictability of phase-modulated severity.}
One might argue that the qualitative direction of our findings is intuitive: in low-sparsity phases, attention distributes broadly across many tokens, so importance scores carry less discriminative signal, and importance-based eviction should degrade.
We do not dispute this intuition.
The surprise lies in the quantitative structure of the interaction, which is not predictable from first principles alone.

First, the \emph{magnitude} of the severity gradient---$11$--$42\times$ amplification % PENDING-BF16
across sparsity levels (Table~\ref{tab:bootstrap})---far exceeds what a naive ``less discriminative $\Rightarrow$ somewhat worse'' argument would predict.
A reviewer expecting a $2$--$3\times$ effect would find an order-of-magnitude amplification difficult to anticipate without measurement.
Second, the gradient is \emph{phase-specific}: compound interaction concentrates in low-sparsity phases while high-sparsity phases exhibit near-additive behavior ($\widetilde{\mathrm{II}}_{\text{high}} < 1$ at all sparsity levels). % PENDING-BF16
This asymmetry means that importance-based eviction is not uniformly fragile---it is selectively fragile in a phase-dependent manner.
Third, and most strikingly, a \emph{crossover} emerges: at $s \geq 0.25$, importance-based eviction \emph{outperforms} random eviction in high-sparsity phases ($\widetilde{\mathrm{II}} = 0.58$ vs.\ $3.00$) % PENDING-BF16
yet \emph{underperforms} dramatically in low-sparsity phases ($\widetilde{\mathrm{II}} = 30.9$ vs.\ $2.9$). % PENDING-BF16
The same strategy reverses direction across phases---a phenomenon that cannot be derived from the observation that ``importance scores are noisier when attention is diffuse.''

\paragraph{Implications for compound sparsity deployment.}
Our findings suggest that the standard practice of applying a uniform compression budget across all inference steps is suboptimal for reasoning models.
Compound severity is not distributed evenly: it concentrates in low-sparsity phases, where the entropy-discrimination collapse mechanism (\S\ref{sec:analysis}) renders importance-based eviction unreliable.
A deployment pipeline that allocates the same sparsity level $s$ to every token position implicitly accepts order-of-magnitude severity penalties during the exploratory reasoning stages that happen to fall in the low-sparsity regime.

This observation motivates \emph{phase-aware compression budgets}: rather than a single global sparsity target, the system would allocate higher capacity (lower sparsity) to low-sparsity phases---where compound interaction is most severe---and reclaim that budget in high-sparsity phases, where compound behavior is near-additive and importance-based eviction remains effective.
The severity gradient $G$ reported in \S\ref{sec:phase-amplification} provides a natural signal for such allocation: phases with $G \gg 1$ receive a reduced sparsity budget, while phases with $G \leq 1$ tolerate aggressive compression with minimal quality loss.

\paragraph{Future directions.}
The phase-aware allocation principle above points toward a concrete system design: a \emph{phase-gated controller} that monitors attention sparsity statistics in real time and dynamically adjusts the compound sparsity budget per reasoning phase.
The controller would route each generation step through a low-overhead phase classifier (\S\ref{sec:phase-seg}), then apply a phase-specific sparsity configuration derived from the severity gradient.
Whether such a controller can recover most of the compression benefit while avoiding the severity amplification in low-sparsity phases is an open empirical question.

A second direction concerns mechanism validation.
The entropy-discrimination collapse hypothesis (\S\ref{sec:analysis}) makes testable predictions about attention entropy redistribution under head pruning.
Directly measuring per-head entropy shifts across phases---and correlating them with the observed compound severity---would provide causal evidence beyond the correlational structure reported here.

Finally, scaling the empirical methodology to larger models and diverse reasoning tasks would establish the generality of the phase-strategy interaction documented in this work.

\subsection{Limitations}
\label{sec:limitations}

\paragraph{Model scale.}
All experiments are conducted at the 7B parameter scale.
Whether the phase-modulated severity patterns persist, amplify, or attenuate at larger scales (e.g., 70B) remains untested.
Larger models may exhibit different attention redundancy structures that alter the entropy-discrimination collapse dynamics.

\paragraph{Architectural scope.}
Our two models---DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct---share the Qwen2ForCausalLM architecture.
The cross-model replication (\S\ref{sec:cross-model}) confirms that the findings are not artifacts of a single model's weights, but both models share the same attention mechanism design.
The entropy-discrimination collapse mechanism is in principle architecture-agnostic (it depends on attention redistribution, not architecture-specific components), but empirical validation on architecturally distinct models (e.g., Mamba-based or mixture-of-experts architectures) is needed.

\paragraph{Task coverage.}
We evaluate exclusively on MATH-500, a mathematical reasoning benchmark.
Different reasoning tasks---code generation, commonsense reasoning, multi-hop question answering---may induce different phase structures with different sparsity distributions, potentially altering the severity gradient profile.
Generalizing the phase-strategy interaction to broader reasoning domains is an important next step.

\paragraph{No throughput evaluation.}
This work focuses on characterizing the \emph{structural} properties of compound sparsity severity---its phase dependence, strategy dependence, and interaction magnitude.
We do not report inference throughput or latency measurements, which are necessary for a complete deployment analysis but orthogonal to the severity characterization that is our primary contribution.

# ============================================================
# 投稿目标
# ============================================================
target:
  venue: EMNLP 2026 ARR
  deadline: 2026-05-25
  days_remaining: 11
  format: long paper (8 pages + references + appendix)
  anonymization: ARR double-blind

# ============================================================
# Paper Outline
# ============================================================
outline:
  title_candidates:
    - "Phase-Modulated Compound Sparsity: How Eviction Strategy and Reasoning Phase Interact in Sparse LLM Inference"
    - "Emergent Phase-Strategy Interaction in Compound Sparse LLM Inference"
    - "When Compound Sparsity Bites Back: Phase-Dependent Severity Amplification in Importance-Based Eviction"

  sections:
    - id: abstract
      title: Abstract
      summary: >
        Compound sparsity (head pruning + KV cache eviction) is assumed to degrade uniformly.
        We show the interaction is strategy-dependent and phase-modulated: importance-based eviction
        exhibits 12-75× severity amplification in low-sparsity reasoning phases, while random eviction
        stays flat (~1×). Bootstrap CI (B=10000) confirms significance at all 4 sparsity levels (p<0.0001).
        Cross-model replication on Qwen2.5-7B validates generalizability. We explain this via an
        entropy-discrimination collapse mechanism: head pruning distributes surviving attention,
        destroying importance score discriminability specifically in distributed-attention phases.
      length: 250 words

    - id: introduction
      title: "1. Introduction"
      summary: >
        Motivate compound sparsity as practical deployment need. State gap: prior work (SparK, Ada-KV)
        treats compound interaction as uniformly super-additive. Our finding: the severity is an
        emergent property of the interaction between eviction strategy and reasoning phase.
        Preview crossover phenomenon and mechanism. State contributions.
      length: 1 page
      key_claims:
        - Compound sparsity severity is not uniform — it is strategy-dependent and phase-modulated
        - Importance-based eviction amplifies compound interaction 12-75× in low-sparsity phases
        - Entropy-discrimination collapse explains the phase-strategy interaction

    - id: related_work
      title: "2. Related Work"
      summary: >
        Three threads: (1) Compound/joint compression (SparK, SLiM, UniComp, compression-ordering)
        — none analyzes phase × strategy interaction. (2) KV cache eviction (Ada-KV, DefensiveKV,
        SnapKV, NACL) — importance fragility noted but not phase-conditioned. (3) Phase-aware
        inference (ThinKV, PagedEviction, reasoning dynamics) — single-axis, no compound interaction.
      length: 0.75 page
      key_refs:
        - spark-aaai2026
        - thinkv-iclr2026
        - defensivekv-iclr2026
        - slim-icml2025
        - phase-transition-compression-2026
        - decision-repr-transition-2026
        - retentivekv-2026
        - greedy-bias-kvcache-2026

    - id: background
      title: "3. Background and Problem Setup"
      summary: >
        Define compound sparsity (attention head pruning ⊗ KV cache eviction). Define Interaction
        Index (II) measuring super/sub-additivity. Define phase segmentation via ThinKV-style
        token-ratio method. Formalize the research question: is II constant across phases and strategies?
      length: 1 page
      subsections:
        - "3.1 Compound Sparsity Formulation"
        - "3.2 Interaction Index"
        - "3.3 Phase Segmentation"

    - id: methodology
      title: "4. Experimental Setup"
      summary: >
        Models (DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct), dataset (MATH-500 subset, 50 problems),
        sparsity levels (s=0.15/0.20/0.25/0.30), eviction strategies (importance-based cumulative
        attention with position normalization, random), metrics (PPL, II, gradient), hardware.
        Statistical method: per-problem bootstrap CI (B=10000), paired and unpaired.
      length: 1 page

    - id: results
      title: "5. Results"
      summary: >
        Main finding: importance gradient 11-42× (problem-level bootstrap) increasing with sparsity,
        random gradient ~1×. Bootstrap CI all significant (p<0.001 fp16, target p<10⁻⁴ bf16).
        Crossover: importance safer than random in high-sparsity phase but dramatically worse in
        low-sparsity phase. Sub-exponential growth pattern. Cross-model replication on Qwen.
      length: 2.5 pages
      subsections:
        - "5.0 Experimental Overview (sec:exp-overview)"
        - "5.1 Strategy-Dependent Severity — C1 (sec:strategy-severity)"
        - "5.2 Phase-Modulated Amplification — C2 (sec:phase-amplification)"
        - "5.3 Phase-Strategy Crossover — C3 (sec:crossover)"
        - "5.4 Cross-Model Replication — C5 (sec:cross-model)"
        - "5.5 Statistical Validation (sec:stat-validation)"

    - id: analysis
      title: "6. Analysis: Entropy-Discrimination Collapse"
      summary: >
        Mechanistic explanation: head pruning → surviving heads attend more uniformly → importance
        score entropy increases → discrimination between important/unimportant KV entries collapses →
        importance-based eviction degrades to biased pseudo-random in distributed-attention phases.
        This is phase-dependent because reasoning phases have more distributed attention.
      length: 1 page

    - id: discussion
      title: "7. Discussion"
      summary: >
        Implications for compound sparsity deployment: uniform budgets are unsafe.
        Phase-gated controllers as solution direction. Limitations: 7B models only,
        MATH-500 only, no throughput measurements yet.
      length: 0.5 page

    - id: conclusion
      title: "8. Conclusion"
      summary: >
        Compound sparsity severity is an emergent property of strategy × phase interaction.
        This finding challenges the implicit assumption of uniform compound degradation
        and motivates phase-aware sparsity allocation.
      length: 0.25 page

\section{Discussion}
\label{sec:discussion}

\paragraph{On the predictability of phase-modulated severity.}
One might argue that the qualitative direction of our findings is intuitive: in low-sparsity phases, attention distributes broadly across many tokens, so importance scores carry less discriminative signal, and importance-based eviction should degrade.
We do not dispute this intuition.
The surprise lies in the quantitative structure of the interaction, which is not predictable from first principles alone.

First, the \emph{magnitude} of the severity gradient---$11$--$42\times$ amplification % PENDING-BF16
across sparsity levels (Table~\ref{tab:bootstrap})---far exceeds what a naive ``less discriminative $\Rightarrow$ somewhat worse'' argument would predict.
A reviewer expecting a $2$--$3\times$ effect would find an order-of-magnitude amplification difficult to anticipate without measurement.
Second, the gradient is \emph{phase-specific}: compound interaction concentrates in low-sparsity phases while high-sparsity phases exhibit near-additive behavior ($\widetilde{\mathrm{II}}_{\text{high}} < 1$ at all sparsity levels). % PENDING-BF16
This asymmetry means that importance-based eviction is not uniformly fragile---it is selectively fragile in a phase-dependent manner.
Third, and most strikingly, a \emph{crossover} emerges: at $s \geq 0.25$, importance-based eviction \emph{outperforms} random eviction in high-sparsity phases ($\widetilde{\mathrm{II}} = 0.58$ vs.\ $3.00$) % PENDING-BF16
yet \emph{underperforms} dramatically in low-sparsity phases ($\widetilde{\mathrm{II}} = 30.9$ vs.\ $2.9$). % PENDING-BF16
The same strategy reverses direction across phases---a phenomenon that cannot be derived from the observation that ``importance scores are noisier when attention is diffuse.''

\paragraph{Implications for compound sparsity deployment.}
Our findings suggest that the standard practice of applying a uniform compression budget across all inference steps is suboptimal for reasoning models.
Compound severity is not distributed evenly: it concentrates in low-sparsity phases, where the entropy-discrimination collapse mechanism (\S\ref{sec:analysis}) renders importance-based eviction unreliable.
A deployment pipeline that allocates the same sparsity level $s$ to every token position implicitly accepts order-of-magnitude severity penalties during the exploratory reasoning stages that happen to fall in the low-sparsity regime.

This observation motivates \emph{phase-aware compression budgets}: rather than a single global sparsity target, the system would allocate higher capacity (lower sparsity) to low-sparsity phases---where compound interaction is most severe---and reclaim that budget in high-sparsity phases, where compound behavior is near-additive and importance-based eviction remains effective.
The severity gradient $G$ reported in \S\ref{sec:phase-amplification} provides a natural signal for such allocation: phases with $G \gg 1$ receive a reduced sparsity budget, while phases with $G \leq 1$ tolerate aggressive compression with minimal quality loss.

\paragraph{Future directions.}
The phase-aware allocation principle above points toward a concrete system design: a \emph{phase-gated controller} that monitors attention sparsity statistics in real time and dynamically adjusts the compound sparsity budget per reasoning phase.
The controller would route each generation step through a low-overhead phase classifier (\S\ref{sec:phase-seg}), then apply a phase-specific sparsity configuration derived from the severity gradient.
Whether such a controller can recover most of the compression benefit while avoiding the severity amplification in low-sparsity phases is an open empirical question.

A second direction concerns mechanism validation.
The entropy-discrimination collapse hypothesis (\S\ref{sec:analysis}) makes testable predictions about attention entropy redistribution under head pruning.
Directly measuring per-head entropy shifts across phases---and correlating them with the observed compound severity---would provide causal evidence beyond the correlational structure reported here.

Finally, scaling the empirical methodology to larger models and diverse reasoning tasks would establish the generality of the phase-strategy interaction documented in this work.

\subsection{Limitations}
\label{sec:limitations}

\paragraph{Model scale.}
All experiments are conducted at the 7B parameter scale.
Whether the phase-modulated severity patterns persist, amplify, or attenuate at larger scales (e.g., 70B) remains untested.
Larger models may exhibit different attention redundancy structures that alter the entropy-discrimination collapse dynamics.

\paragraph{Architectural scope.}
Our two models---DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct---share the Qwen2ForCausalLM architecture.
The cross-model replication (\S\ref{sec:cross-model}) confirms that the findings are not artifacts of a single model's weights, but both models share the same attention mechanism design.
The entropy-discrimination collapse mechanism is in principle agnostic across attention architectures (it depends on attention redistribution, not architecture-specific components), but empirical validation on architecturally distinct attention designs (e.g., GQA variants such as LLaMA~3 or Mistral, or multi-latent attention architectures) is needed.

\paragraph{Task coverage.}
We evaluate exclusively on MATH-500, a mathematical reasoning benchmark.
Different reasoning tasks---code generation, commonsense reasoning, multi-hop question answering---may induce different phase structures with different sparsity distributions, potentially altering the severity gradient profile.
Generalizing the phase-strategy interaction to broader reasoning domains is an important next step.

\paragraph{No throughput evaluation.}
This work focuses on characterizing the \emph{structural} properties of compound sparsity severity---its phase dependence, strategy dependence, and interaction magnitude.
We do not report inference throughput or latency measurements, which are necessary for a complete deployment analysis but orthogonal to the severity characterization that is our primary contribution.

1	\section{Introduction}
2	\label{sec:introduction}
3	
4	Long-context language models place acute pressure on the key--value (KV) cache, which grows linearly with sequence length and dominates inference memory at scale \cite{kwon2023vllm, pope2023efficiently}.
5	Two complementary responses have emerged: \emph{attention head pruning}, which removes structurally redundant heads \cite{voita2019heads, michel2019sixteen}, and \emph{KV cache eviction}, which discards low-importance token positions from the cache \cite{snapkv-neurips2024, adakv-neurips2025}.
6	Deploying both simultaneously---\emph{compound sparsity}---is attractive because the compression gains multiply, but the resulting quality degradation can be super-additive: the joint loss exceeds the sum of individual losses \cite{spark-aaai2026, slim-icml2025}.

14	This \emph{severity gradient} grows monotonically with the sparsity budget: on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, the median phase difference in Interaction Index rises from $0.39$ at $s{=}0.15$ to $14.59$ at $s{=}0.30$, with paired effect sizes increasing from $d{=}0.44$ (small) to $d{=}0.80$ (large); Bonferroni-corrected permutation tests confirm significance at all four sparsity levels on this model ($p < 0.005$).

16	Critically, random eviction produces no such gradient: all four sparsity levels fail to exhibit a significant phase difference, confirming that the severity gradient is an emergent property of the interaction between importance scoring and phase-dependent attention structure, not an artifact of compound sparsity per se.

Our central finding is that it is, and strongly so: under importance-based KV cache eviction, the Interaction Index---a measure of super-additive compound degradation---is concentrated in the low-sparsity phase (where attention distributes broadly) and largely absent in the high-sparsity phase (where attention is focused).
This \emph{severity gradient} grows monotonically with the sparsity budget: on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, the median phase difference in Interaction Index rises from $0.39$ at $s{=}0.15$ to $14.59$ at $s{=}0.30$, with paired effect sizes increasing from $d{=}0.44$ (small) to $d{=}0.80$ (large); Bonferroni-corrected permutation tests confirm significance at all four sparsity levels on this model ($p < 0.005$).
The pattern replicates at $s \geq 0.20$ on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct ($d \geq 0.55$) with attenuated absolute magnitude, though the effect at $s{=}0.15$ does not reach significance ($d{=}0.28$, CI spanning zero).
Critically, random eviction produces no such gradient: all four sparsity levels fail to exhibit a significant phase difference, confirming that the severity gradient is an emergent property of the interaction between importance scoring and phase-dependent attention structure, not an artifact of compound sparsity per se.
